subject: Civil Engineering
title: Hydration: How Cement Hardens
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Hydration: How Cement Hardens.

hook.text: Concrete doesn't dry — it cures. A chemical reaction creates the hardness, not evaporation.

buildup.text: Cement reacts with water to form calcium silicate hydrate — a gel that bonds everything.

discovery.text: Hydration generates heat. In massive pours, the center can reach 160°F — cracking risk rises.

twist.text: Concrete gains strength for decades. At 28 days it reaches design strength — not final strength.

climax.text: The Hoover Dam's concrete is still curing — it generates measurable heat to this day.

punchline.text: Concrete never dries. It hardens through chemistry — and it never fully stops.

quiz.question: Why can large concrete pours crack during curing?
options: The concrete dries too quickly on the surface
The hydration reaction generates heat that causes thermal expansion and cracking
Too much water evaporates from the center of the pour

details.summary: Cement hydration is the exothermic chemical reaction between cement and water that produces calcium silicate hydrate gel and calcium hydroxide. This gel grows into the spaces between cement grains, binding aggregates together and developing strength over weeks, months, and years.
details.whyItMatters: Hydration, not drying or evaporation, is what makes concrete hard. Understanding hydration is critical because temperature, moisture, and time during curing directly control the final strength achieved.
takeaways: Hydration is a chemical reaction, not simply water evashing away
Calcium silicate hydrate gel is the main product responsible for strength
Concrete continues gaining strength for years as hydration progresses slowly

faq.question: Why does concrete continue getting stronger for years after placement?
faq.answer: Hydration is a gradual process. At 28 days, only about 70 to 80% of cement has reacted. The remaining unhydrated cement continues reacting slowly for years if moisture is available. Concrete can reach 150% of its 28-day strength after several years of continued hydration.

faq.question: Why is the hydration reaction exothermic and when does this matter?
faq.answer: Breaking and reforming chemical bonds releases heat energy. In thin structures, this heat dissipates harmlessly. In massive pours like dams, the heat can raise internal temperatures above 70 degrees Celsius, causing thermal cracking as the interior cools and contracts against the cooler surface.
